title: Senegal boat disaster: Dozens missing as migrant boat sinks
description: Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat said to be carrying between 50 and 100 migrants capsized in the Atlantic Ocean.Fo
body: Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat said to be carrying between 50 and 100 migrants capsized in the Atlantic Ocean.Four bodies have reportedly been recovered so far. Dozens of people are still missing.Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT)."Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, AFP reported.However, a local official told Reuters news agency it was carrying 50 people, adding that the boat hit a rock as migrants were transferring from small fishing boats to a larger vessel.Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school enrolment document.At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.Many thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty in recent years.The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone.It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.The Senegalese navy said it had rescued more than 1,400 people on Monday and Tuesday this week.As it has become more difficult to reach Europe through North Africa, due to tighter controls and increased co-operation with European countries, migrants are increasingly targeting Spain's Canary Islands.They often travel in wooden boats known as pirogues that are frequently overloaded and not suited to such long voyages across the Atlantic Ocean.Most migrants arriving in the Canary Islands this year are from Senegal, according to the UN.They are driven to leave home by limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks, according to the IOM.On 7 November, El Hierro, one of the Canary Islands, declared a state of emergency following a surge in migrant arrivals.It said more than 3,300 people had reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of the month. This amounts to almost a third of the island's population.

schema.headline: Senegal boat disaster: Dozens missing as migrant boat sinks

title: Putin vows 'far more painful' response to Ukraine's strikes on Crimean Bridge
description: Moscow's retaliation for attacks on the Crimean Bridge will be "far more painful" than Kyiv's strikes, Vladimir Putin has vowed.In the early hours of
body: Moscow's retaliation for attacks on the Crimean Bridge will be "far more painful" than Kyiv's strikes, Vladimir Putin has vowed.In the early hours of Thursday, the double-arched, 12-mile bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea was hit for a third time this week.A combined missile-and-drone strike on Tuesday destroyed the central road section of the bridge, collapsing part of it into the water and rendering it unusable for road traffic. But at a press conference after historic talks with his Chinese and US counterparts in Shenzhen, Russian president Putin said Moscow's response would be even more significant.Putin claimed the bridge was used exclusively for civilian purposes and not to transport military equipment, as Kyiv has alleged, or petroleum products.Since illegally annexing the Crimean Peninsula in 2014, Moscow has used it as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles. From there it has also carried out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplied its troops in southern Ukraine. Commenting on the strikes on the bridge, Kyiv's defence ministry said that for Ukraine, they amounted to to "time gained and lives saved. The less that reaches the occupiers, the less hits our warriors."The collapse of the Crimean Bridge's arch was the worst damage to be inflicted onto the structure in several years. The bridge had long been in Ukraine's sights because it represents Moscow's pretensions over sovereign Ukrainian land, and because of its logistical importance in supplying Russian troops in the occupied Ukrainian southern regions. It was built and unveiled to great fanfare in 2018, four years after Russia illegally annexed Ukraine's Crimea. Thursday's strike was carried out with Neptune cruise missiles, Ukraine said. Russia's transport ministry said nobody had been hurt in the attack, and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge. Train services on the bridge were suspended but resumed in the afternoon.Car traffic, however, will be prohibited for the foreseeable future as a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was dragged below into the sea when missiles hit the arch on Tuesday.President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making. The seven-stage operation first required the destruction of air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets which protected the bridge. Missiles and drones then dealt the structure the final blow.

schema.headline: Putin vows 'far more painful' response to Ukraine's strikes on Crimean Bridge

title: Mrima Hill deal: US consortium wins Kenya mining project, beating Chinese rivals
description: A US-led consortium, Frontier Minerals, has won the tender to develop Kenya's Mrima Hill mining project, beating seven bidders, including companies fr
body: A US-led consortium, Frontier Minerals, has won the tender to develop Kenya's Mrima Hill mining project, beating seven bidders, including companies from China and Australia.The site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (£45bn), including niobium, used in electric vehicles, aerospace and defence technology.Frontier Minerals says its proposal aims to keep more of the economic benefits in Kenya through "processing and refining of minerals in-country".The deal comes as Washington seeks greater access to Africa's minerals, aiming to strengthen US supply chains and compete with China.Frontier Minerals brings together three US companies - Bunker Hill Mining Corp, American Resources Corporation and ReElement Technologies Corporation. The consortium combines expertise in mineral resource development, critical materials supply chains and advanced refining technologies.A central part of its proposal is to develop mineral processing and refining capacity in Kenya. Brad Barnett from Frontier Minerals said the company wanted the country to capture more value from its mineral resources.Mrima Hill is located in Kwale County, near Kenya's Indian Ocean coastline. The site covers about 390 acres of forest.The prospect of mining in the area has raised concerns among local residents, who fear the project could damage the forest and threaten their ancestral heritage. There are also questions over whether communities living near the site will benefit from the investment.Barnett was keen to reassure Kenyans that they would benefit: "We intend to create lasting opportunities for Kenyan workers, businesses and the wider economy through capacity-building and targeted investment, while prioritising environmental management and performance."The consortium must still obtain a prospecting licence and meet the necessary regulatory requirements before the project can proceed.The tender decision has drawn objections from competing bidders. Reuters news agency reports that two rival companies intend to challenge the selection, with Australia's RareX alleging that Frontier Minerals missed an earlier submission deadline. Kenya's government has maintained that the process was open and transparent.The project comes as US strives to secure alternative sources of critical minerals and reduce dependence on China, which dominates the processing of several key minerals.Washington has been pursuing partnerships with mineral-rich African countries, including the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, as it seeks to strengthen supply chains for industries ranging from electric vehicles to defence technology.Kenya's mining ministry says the sector is an important part of its plans to diversify the economy beyond traditional sources of revenue such as tourism, agriculture and financial services.

schema.headline: Mrima Hill deal: US consortium wins Kenya mining project, beating Chinese rivals

title: Bududa landslide: Ugandan survivors  seek justice at the UN
description: ByOndiro Oganga and Swaibu IbrahimBBC AfricaReporting fromKampalaSurvivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have
body: ByOndiro Oganga and Swaibu IbrahimBBC AfricaReporting fromKampalaSurvivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides.Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods.The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking  climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.At least 33 of the 53 people who died in the 2019 landslide were children. Years later, survivors say every spell of heavy rain brings back fears of another tragedy.William Tsama, one of the claimants, lost four members of his family."My quest should be a lesson," he said. "Victims in such situations, ignored by governments, can take them to court to compel them to help their citizens." Uganda introduced a resettlement plan for landslide-prone areas in 2011, but progress has been limited, with relatively few people relocated.Last month, it launched a new resettlement programme offering affected households 18m Ugandan shillings ($4,300; £3,300) to help them move to safer areas.But some survivors have questioned whether the amount is enough to cover the cost of relocating and rebuilding their lives.Under the programme, families can choose between receiving two acres of land, valued at 8m shillings, plus 10m shillings  towards building a house, or taking the equivalent land allowance in cash, alongside the same housing grant.The scheme is expected to benefit 1,410 households identified as living in high-risk areas.The government has now given residents of designated high-risk areas two months, from November to December, to leave or face forced eviction.The threat extends beyond landslides. The complainants say changing rainfall patterns and declining soil fertility have also affected farming, leaving many families struggling to secure their livelihoods."I want to get a new good place for my people, so even if I die, they will be okay. I am an old man, but I am doing it for my children," Tsama said.The survivors first launched legal action in 2020 in Uganda, and received support from Ugandan environmental organisation Greenwatch three years later.They are seeking compensation for lost family members and livelihoods, as well as emergency measures, including accessible early-warning systems in high-risk areas.Greenwatch Executive Director Samantha Atukunda Kakuru Mwesigwa said the case is about changing how governments prepare and respond to climate-related disasters."Justice for claimants is not just about winning in court. It is about forcing government policy to keep pace with a changing climate, and ensuring loss and damage is no longer an afterthought in disaster management," she said.The threat of climate-related disasters extends across East Africa.In Kenya, floods and landslides killed at least 181 people between March and May 2024, according to the Kenya Red Cross. In Rwanda, floods and landslides killed 135 people in May 2023.The dangers are also being felt further afield. In October 2026, a flash flood swept through Nepal's Gorkha district after a landslide blocked a river, washing away homes and infrastructure, and killing over 1,500 people."Disasters like the one in Bududa are only getting worse because of climate change – and they are happening all around the world, as we've seen recently and tragically in Nepal," ClientEarth lawyer Vesselina Newman said.She said poorer countries, which have contributed relatively little to global  emissions, are bearing some of the heaviest consequences of climate change and need greater financial support."High income countries must provide financial assistance and ensure that sufficient money goes directly to countries like Uganda, so they can roll out life-saving adaptation measures," she said.The complainants say relocation must involve more than moving people out of danger.They want the government to protect their livelihoods, respect their land rights, and take account of individual needs.The case is now before the United Nations Human Rights Committee, which will ask the Ugandan government to respond within six months.More Uganda stories on BBC:

schema.headline: Bududa landslide: Ugandan survivors  seek justice at the UN

title: Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island
description: Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.The drone attack on Ku
body: Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. The Iranian army said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase, which hosts US forces, but Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage.It came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials.Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on Tuesday.The recent exchanges of fire, as well as deadlock in negotiations on a peace deal, have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war.The conflict began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.Since then, Iran has retaliated for US and Israeli strikes by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.It has also attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.On Tuesday night, Kuwait's military said its air defences engaged "drone threats" but did not report any casualties or damage.The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, saying it "flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law"."The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying," Hani Mohammed, an Egyptian resident of Kuwait, told AFP news agency.Bahrain's military also said on Wednesday that its air defence systems had "intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks".The island kingdom, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, has reported four attacks over the past six days, following a two-month lull.Qatar, which has mediated in the stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, said the Iranian attacks on its neighbours were a "dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions".The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait.Later, the army's commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned the US and its allies that it would respond more forcefully to any new attacks on Iran."If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said.On Tuesday night, US fighter jets targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island "with precision munitions" in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets", US military officials said.Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they had caused no damage to infrastructure.In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a search-and-rescue operation was under way for a missing sailor following an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated and 11 were receiving medical care, it added.The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles (24km) north of Khasab, in Oman's Musandam peninsula. It said the attack caused a fire on board that was extinguished.Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG) had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an "authorised route".At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.In recent months, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz, allowing crude oil exports from Gulf states to reach around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts.

schema.headline: Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island

title: Falcon 6X: Why Ghana is facing backlash over new $60m presidential jet
description: Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.Par
body: Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.Parliament approved its purchase last December as part of a broader programme to modernise Ghana's military aviation fleet, which also includes four helicopters from Airbus.The jet was welcomed with a water salute on Monday, but its arrival triggered criticism online and among opposition politicians over the cost and timing of the purchase. While in the opposition, Mahama himself opposed buying a new presidential jet, prompting questions about why his administration has now gone head with the purchase.Opposition MP Samuel Abu Jinapor questioned the government's priorities, saying the expenditure came at a time when many Ghanaians continue to struggle with the cost of living and youth unemployment remained alarmingly high."What was unacceptable in opposition cannot suddenly become acceptable in government merely because the occupants of power have changed," Jinapor added. He accused the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) of hypocrisy, recalling how its senior figures had strongly opposed proposals for a new presidential aircraft when they were in opposition.Jinapor also called for greater transparency over the procurement process, how the purchase was financed and the government's justification for the expenditure.The purchase has also prompted sharp criticism on social media, with some users arguing the money could have been spent on more pressing public needs."This money can employ over 100,000 nurses and 200,000 teachers," an X user posted. But the government has rejected the criticism, saying Ghana's economic circumstances have changed considerably since the NDC opposed a similar purchase.Peter Lanchene Toobu, chairman of parliament's defence committee, said the party had never opposed acquiring a presidential jet in principle. Its objection, he said, had been on the timing when Ghana was experiencing severe economic difficulties."We agreed in principle that we needed to purchase a new presidential jet," he said.He argued, however, that Ghana could not justify the expenditure at a time when it was seeking a $3bn bailout from the IMF."The strength and macroeconomic stability of this country have enhanced our status in the sense that imports have become cheaper, and this is the right time," he added.Toobu said the government had purchased the aircraft without borrowing, citing a stronger Ghanaian currency and improved economic conditions.Government spokesperson Kwakye Ofosu also dismissed suggestions that the purchase was a misplaced priority.He pointed to falling prices of construction materials and lower borrowing costs as evidence of the country's improved economic situation."When I was campaigning in 2024, and I was donating cement, it cost 115 cedis (£7.5) a bag. Today, for 80 cedis, you will get a bag of cement," he told JoyNews.The controversy has also extended to the aircraft's interior, following claims that it has a dedicated bedroom and bathroom.But Ofosu dismissed claims that the jet had such luxury facilities, saying the president has no intention of "bathing in the air"."There certainly is no bathroom. President Mahama has no intention of bathing in the air," Ofosu said.He explained that the jet has reclining seats that can be converted into sleeping arrangements but denied that it has a dedicated bedroom.The government says the new jet will replace the 16-year-old Falcon 900EX, which has suffered recurring maintenance problems, including corrosion and leakages in its fuel tank.The older jet was reportedly grounded in France for several months in 2025 while undergoing repairs.Officials say the Falcon 6X has a longer flying range, reducing the need for refuelling stops on international trips and improving the reliability of presidential travel.Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin, an economist at the University of Ghana said that while the president's safety was paramount, the timing of the purchase was difficult to justify amid severe austerity measures, high unemployment and widespread infrastructure challenges."The timing makes it a bit difficult to understand," he told the BBC, adding that the government should provide a cost-benefit analysis explaining why buying the jet was preferable to leasing one and how the decision serves Ghana's interests.Additional reporting by Thomas Naadi in Accra

schema.headline: Falcon 6X: Why Ghana is facing backlash over new $60m presidential jet

title: Julio Iglesias faces court investigation over alleged sexual offences
description: Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff m
body: Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff membersTwo women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations.But in a statement published on Wednesday, external (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio Piña said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment. But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. Piña said these allegations were dismissed after he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".Piña said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February. The announcement comes after Spain's public prosecutor's office shifted its position last month, saying it now believed the court had jurisdiction to investigate the allegations. In its statement, the national court said Spanish law sets out that courts can hear cases of crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens provided certain conditions are met.The allegations against Iglesias first emerged in a joint three-year investigation between Spanish newspaper El Diario, external and television network Univision news, published in January.In that investigation, the two women were identified as a domestic worker and a physical therapist, who described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions. The domestic worker, whose name was changed to Rebeca in the reports, said Iglesias would regularly call her to his room at the end of the day and would touch her inappropriately without consent.Rebeca, a Dominican who was 22 when the alleged events took place, also alleged that Iglesias had forced her to take part in threesomes with another female member of staff. She also described the singer slapping her in the face and grabbing her genitals.The other woman, a Venezuelan physical therapist named as Laura in the article, said Iglesias had touched her breasts and kissed her on the mouth against her will. She added that he constantly threatened to fire her, controlled how much food she ate and asked her about when her period was due.Rebeca and Laura filed an initial legal complaint in January against Iglesias for sexual assault and human trafficking.In a response to the allegations in January, Iglesias said, external: "I deny having abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman. These accusations are absolutely false and deeply sadden me."On Wednesday, the court said the lawsuit had been accepted based on evidence provided in the complaint. This included a photograph of one of the complainants, showing a bruise on her arm that was "consistent with the possibility of her being grabbed forcefully".It added that the same photo showed "two marks on one of her thighs that could correspond to a human bite", which the complainant said were "a consequence of her forced participation in acts of a sexual nature".WhatsApp message exchanges, including New Year's greetings, which suggest an "affectionate" relationship between the women and Iglesias, will also be considered, the court said.But it added that the seemingly cordial tone, which presents "an apparent discrepancy with certain aspects of the narrative", would be clarified through a "complete and contextualised examination of the communications".The claim over violations of workers' rights could not be investigated because there is no comparable criminal offence in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic, where the alleged crimes took place, it said.Iglesias is one of the most successful Latin artists of all time, having sold more than 300 million records in a career spanning decades.He is also the father of fellow music superstar Enrique Iglesias.

schema.headline: Julio Iglesias faces court investigation over alleged sexual offences

title: Venezuela signs military deal with US less than a year after Maduro's removal
description: The United States and Venezuela have re-established military ties less than a year after US forces seized the then-leader of the South American countr
body: The United States and Venezuela have re-established military ties less than a year after US forces seized the then-leader of the South American country, Nicolás Maduro, in a raid on the capital, Caracas.The interim government led by Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro's former vice-president, signed a military co-operation agreement with US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth on Wednesday.Few details about the deal have been released so far but Hegseth said that Venezuela had "gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner" in less than 12 months. Interim President Rodríguez said the deal would help confront "common threats".Military co-operation between the two countries was terminated in 2005 by Hugo Chávez, Venezuela's left-wing president at the time.Chávez alleged that US military personnel sent to Venezuela to train their counterparts had made disparaging remarks about his government. He also accused the US military office located in Fuerte Tiuna, Venezuela's largest military complex, of being "an organ of the CIA... conspiring against the government". Under Nicolás Maduro, who succeeded Chávez after the latter's death from cancer, relations between the two countries deteriorated further.They reached rock bottom late last year when the US doubled its reward for information leading to Maduro's capture to $50m (£38m) and eventually seized him on 3 January in a military raid. Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are now in custody in New York on charges of drug-trafficking and conspiracy to commit torture, which they deny. Hegseth addressed the change in the two countries' relationship since Maduro was seized in his speech at the US embassy in Caracas on Wednesday. "It's a great honour to be here as the first United States Secretary of War this century to set foot in Venezuela. The weight of this moment does not escape me," he said."Just one year ago, my presence here, our presence here would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable," he added before recalling a public appearance by then-President Maduro which had angered the Trump administration. "Exactly one year ago today, the indicted narco-terrorist fugitive Nicolás Maduro, the man who spent more than a decade handing Venezuela's borders and territory to terrorists from all over the world, stood on a stage, not too far from here, and yelled mockingly: 'Come and get me!'. Well, we answered that call." Hegseth added that the result of the US military raid on 3 January had been as Maduro predicted, quoting the deposed leader's words: "No war, yes peace."He described the deal signed by him and Venezuela's defence minister on Wednesday as a "new chapter for the United States, for Venezuela, for the Venezuelan military and for the Western Hemisphere through the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition".Rodríguez described it as "extraordinarily relevant for our bilateral relations"."In a matter of months, secretary, we have turned very difficult moments for our people into a space for co-operation and mutual benefit for both of our countries," she said addressing Hegseth during a meeting at the presidential palace.While no details of the deal have been published, in her speech Rodríguez mentioned the training of Venezuela's armed forces and improving its "operational equipment" and access to new technology "to confront shared threats".In his speech at the US embassy, Hegseth was more direct about who he considers to be those threats. Addressing "the narco-terrorists who abuse this [Venezuela] as a safe haven", he warned that  "we will hunt you down, we will find you, and we will kill you".From Venezuela, Hegseth travelled on to neighbouring Colombia, whose president, Abelardo de la Espriella, is a close ally of the Trump administration. Colombia is already part of the US-led Americas Counter Cartel Coalition and in August, Hegseth had floated the possibility of joint US-Colombian military operations against armed groups.On Wednesday, President de la Espriella took to X to deny a report by the New York Times which had stated that he had rejected carrying out joint operations, external.In his post, he stressed that any decision would be taken while respecting Colombia's constitution, and the country's laws and sovereignty. Hegseth reposted the tweet commenting that the US-Colombian partnership "is stronger than ever before".

schema.headline: Venezuela signs military deal with US less than a year after Maduro's removal

title: Russian arrested for spying on US defence company Palantir over Ukraine support
description: A Russian man has been arrested in California's Silicon Valley for allegedly attempting to spy on employees of a technology and defence firm that supp
body: A Russian man has been arrested in California's Silicon Valley for allegedly attempting to spy on employees of a technology and defence firm that supports the Ukrainian military.Igor D'iu is accused of acting as an agent of a foreign government to conduct a covert operation in Palo Alto, near San Francisco. The BBC understands that the company targeted was Palantir Technologies. D'iu is also charged with stalking employees and possessing falsified identity documents. The company is not named in charging documents, but is described as a publicly traded technology and defence company that produces software used by Ukraine in its war with Russia."The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian."We will not tolerate any efforts - by foreign governments or otherwise - to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations."Prosecutors say that D'iu entered the US unlawfully via the Mexico border, after travelling there from Istanbul in June.He was allegedly recruited through the Telegram encrypted messaging app. His handlers referred to Russia as "'the Motherland' and directed D'iu to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine". On their instruction, he purchased computers, phones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software - tools he needed for his spy mission.He then went to a coffee shop located near the company's offices in Palo Alto, where he photographed laptop screens of employees who were working there. His handlers also allegedly "instructed him to position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity".A source in the industry confirmed that Palantir was targeted, and added that the operation did not penetrate the company's private systems.They added that the company has been "targeted extensively" by Russia over its involvement in Ukraine, and that the attacks are becoming "increasingly aggressive".The source, who did not want to be named, said that this was the first time a Russian operative was found while on US soil attempting to spy on the company. "I think the surprising thing is that they decided to take the risk of sending someone to the US," they said, in an attempt to get into the system "physically". Palantir has not issued a statement in reaction to the charges.D'iu also allegedly conducted surveillance of employees and their residences. On 3 September, he followed a vehicle driven by one senior executive for nearly 30 miles. He fled after she drove to a police station. Police later obtained evidence that he had followed other employees' cars on previous days.During the investigation, officials discovered identity cards that had been falsified - including a US passport, California ID card, and a Social Security card with the fake name "Hugo Landry Johns".A raid on his home in October in East Palo Alto turned up a handwritten notebook that contained numerous home addresses of employees "family members' names, educational and employment histories, and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses", prosecutors say. Two Russian passports were also found.He faces two charges related his alleged work as a foreign agent, one charge of interstate stalking, and one count of fraud related to his identity documents. He faces over 15 years in prison if found guilty.

schema.headline: Russian arrested for spying on US defence company Palantir over Ukraine support

title: Pew survey: What India's changing Hindu and Muslim populations tell us
description: India's religious make-up - what a new Pew study says about Hindus and MuslimsImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, An Indian woman lights
body: India's religious make-up - what a new Pew study says about Hindus and MuslimsImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, An Indian woman lights lamps on the occasion of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lightsByIndia correspondentIndia will remain overwhelmingly Hindu for decades to come, but its religious composition is projected to shift gradually.A new study by the Pew Research Center, projecting the world's religious populations to 2070, estimates that Hindus will make up 76% of India's population by then, down from 79% in 2020, while the Muslim share will rise from 15% to 20%.The shift is rooted largely in differences in age and fertility: Indian Muslims are younger than Hindus and, on average, have more children.The Pew projections place India at the centre of a wider demographic shift across South Asia. Pakistan is expected to overtake Indonesia as the country with the world's largest Muslim-majority population, with India moving into second place. Bangladesh, too, is projected to see substantial growth in its Muslim population.The study projects the religious composition of the world over the next 50-year period, drawing on data from 201 countries and territories, covering virtually the entire global population.Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, Muslims offer prayer at the historic Jama Masjid in DelhiIt tracks seven religious groups between 2020 and 2070, assuming recent demographic trends continue. Using census and survey data, it establishes each group's size and age profile in 2020, and factors in differences in fertility and religious switching.The findings place India at the heart of a changing global religious landscape. The country is expected to have the world's second-largest Muslim population by 2070, after Pakistan, with about 334 million Muslims. Pakistan itself will overtake Indonesia as the country with the largest Muslim population, with an estimated 461 million.Yet the projections offer little support for the more dramatic narratives sometimes attached to India's changing religious composition. If current demographic trends continue, the Hindu population in the country is expected to grow by 176 million between 2020 and 2070, the report says. It will continue to account for more than three-quarters of the country's population. Despite a sharp fall in India's overall fertility, Muslim women still have more children, on average, than Hindu women. Pew attributes the shift primarily to demographic momentum. Indian Muslims had a median age of 24 in 2020, compared with 29 for Hindus. Between 2025 and 2030, Pew estimates Muslim women in India will have an average of 2.3 children, against 1.8 among Hindu women."We expect religious change in India to be driven almost entirely by long-standing demographic differences between Hindus and Muslims: Muslims are younger and have higher fertility rates," Stephanie Kramer of the Pew Research Center told the BBC.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Hindu devotees offer prayers on the banks of the Sabarmati river in India's Gujarat"The fertility gap has narrowed considerably – from more than one child per woman in 1992 to about half a child in recent years and is likely to keep shrinking," she said."But Hindu fertility is already below the replacement level, while Muslim fertility is projected to remain above it for another two decades." (A replacement level is one at which new births are sufficient to maintain a stable population.)The projections are hardly surprising, says KS James, an Indian demographer at Princeton University."The fertility gap between Muslims and Hindus is well established and it means Muslim population growth is likely to remain faster for the next few decades. But fertility is declining across all religious communities and the gap is expected to narrow further," he told the BBC."Ultimately, they will converge," he says, adding that the projections do not point to anything dramatically different in India's demographic trajectory.Demographers push back against claims, often amplified by Hindu right-wing groups, that Muslims will eventually outnumber Hindus. There is no evidence of any significant religious conversion driving population change in India, they say, and the projections do not support such "alarmist scenarios". Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, Muslim children dressed in festive attire in IndiaThe wider South Asian picture is equally revealing, according to the report. Pakistan's Muslim population is projected to more than double to 461 million by 2070, overtaking Indonesia as the world's largest. India will rank second, with 334 million Muslims, while Bangladesh's Muslim population will rise to 218 million. India and Nepal, meanwhile, will remain the world's only Hindu-majority countries.There appears to be a global story behind these regional shifts.By 2035, Muslims are projected to overtake Christians as the world's largest religious group, according to the report. By 2070, their numbers are expected to reach 3.64 billion, up from 2.02 billion in 2020. Christianity, meanwhile, will have just under three billion followers. Muslims will account for 36% of humanity, compared with 26% today.But the most dramatic transformation may be taking place thousands of miles west of South Asia, in Africa. Christianity's centre of gravity is moving steadily away from Europe and the Americas towards sub-Saharan Africa. The report says that if recent trends continue, more than half of the world's Christians are expected to live there by 2070, compared with 31% in 2020. Pew forecasts that the Democratic Republic of Congo will overtake the United States as the country with the largest Christian population.Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty Images)Image caption, With more than 1.4 billion people, India overtook China in 2023 in terms of population, according to the UNThe steepest decline is expected to occur in Europe. If current trends continue, by 2070 Europe will be home to 11% of the world's Christian population, down from 22% in 2020, the report says.The US is projected to lose its Christian majority by 2065, although Christians will remain the country's largest religious group in 2070. One reason for this changing religious landscape is the growing number of people identifying with no religion.In UK and France, the "religiously unaffiliated" are projected to become the majority by 2070. South Korea is expected to follow suit. Yet their share of the world's population is forecast to fall from 24% to 17%, largely because of a decline in China's population.China accounts for about two-thirds of the world's religiously unaffiliated population. Its expected population decline will more than offset growth in secular populations elsewhere, the report says.By 2070, there are other unexpected shifts. The US is projected to become the world's fifth-largest Hindu population, with immigration driving much of its growth. And Australia's unaffiliated population will overtake Christians as the country's largest group. Buddhism, meanwhile, faces a demographic squeeze. Its population is expected to fall by more than half in China, Japan and South Korea, reflecting the ageing and shrinking populations of East Asia. Laos and Mongolia are projected to lose their Buddhist majorities.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Muslims offer Eid prayers in Pakistan There are, of course, caveats. These are demographic projections, not predictions of everything that might happen. Pew assumes that recently observed patterns of fertility, migration and religious switching - or conversions -  will continue."There are many events that could affect religious group populations (including wars, natural disasters, epidemics and changes in economic or social circumstances) that are not analysed here," the report admits.India's baseline also required projecting the 2020 religious composition from the 2011 census, because the subsequent census had been delayedStill, the broad direction is unmistakable. South Asia will remain indispensable to the world's religious story, not just because of India's enormous Hindu population but because of the growing weight of its Muslim populations. Africa will increasingly shape Christianity's future, while Europe and parts of East Asia become more secular.Clearly, by 2070, the world's religious landscape may look markedly different, shaped less by conversion than by the uneven arithmetic of births, deaths and migration.

schema.headline: Pew survey: What India's changing Hindu and Muslim populations tell us

title: 'Frustrated' - Democrats remain a divided party despite winning big in midterms
description: Those present, who included activists and political organisers, were invigorated and celebratory the week after a "blue tsunami" saw Democrats win in
body: Those present, who included activists and political organisers, were invigorated and celebratory the week after a "blue tsunami" saw Democrats win in Republican heartlands in the midterm elections. The party took control of both chambers of Congress, winning a majority in the House by over 80 seats and gaining nine seats in the Senate.But the atmosphere in Denver was also introspective and forward-looking, as discussions focused on how those victories were won, which issues did not resonate, and what would be needed to continue the party's seat-winning momentum.Some, like Talarico, suggested working alongside Republicans to push forward an economic agenda that would resonate with Americans, such as extending health coverage and reducing inflation.Alabama Congressman Shomari Figures - who surprised many pollsters when he held his seat despite Republicans redrawing his district months before the election - cautioned against going after Trump, when there were more pressing concerns for Americans.Previous Democratic-led efforts to impeach Trump both ended in Senate acquittals."We impeached him twice and got him back - with a Republican majority," Figures said.Yet others, like Maryland Congresswoman Angela Alsobrooks, insisted that voters wanted to see accountability.Voters "realised the smash-and-grab that occurred, and they want people to account for it", she said, pushing for transparent investigations into the Trump administration.The two-day event was staged by Majority Democrats, a political action committee launched last year to address tensions between the left and centrist factions of the party, with some of the biggest divisions forming over how to deliver health care and the war in Gaza. Prominent left-wing members of the party - such as Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator-elect Abdul El Sayed - were not in attendance. In Denver, it was clear those tensions weren't going away, as protesters waving Palestinian flags shouted as people walked past and armed police looked on. Some in attendance made a point to criticise Chuck Schumer, the long-time Democratic Senate minority leader who is seen as a part of the party's centrist establishment. He has been challenged for the role of Senate majority leader by Chris Van Hollen, a senator from Maryland who is considered a left-wing populist.Democrats have not been "strong enough in their displeasure with what's been happening with Trump, and I think that's one of the reasons that people are asking for new leadership," said Vicki Saxe, holding a sign criticising Schumer."I'm frustrated with the lack of urgency that I feel coming from the party leadership," said Tami Butters, 65, standing beside her with a "Vote Yes for Chris Van Hollen" sign. She cited the absence of 11 Democrats last week, when the House voted on whether to consider impeaching US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The effort failed.Hakeem Jeffries, a centrist Democrat who is poised to become the country's first black speaker of the House, faced similar pushback, as protesters heckled his speech.One of the biggest issues of division is the war in Gaza, with both Schumer and Jeffries backing continued military assistance for Israel, while some new members of Congress, like El-Sayed, support ending unconditional US military aid to Israel.Non-profit founder Shiva Saram, who also chairs the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund, travelled from Connecticut to the conference despite having "almost left my party over Gaza and the Iran War".Saram has been newly encouraged, however, by the "real depth in our bench of new and young leaders"."What my party has done wrong for too long is we did not listen," she said.Many speakers and guests stressed that the Democrats won because they focused on real policies that would impact their constituents' daily lives - and that failing to do so in previous years might have been why they lost on those occasions.Delaware Senator Chris Coons told BBC News that he had advised newly elected members to "under-promise and over-deliver"."We got hired because the average American wants us to help make their lives better - lower their costs, end the cruelty and the corruption and give them more reason for hope," he said. "That's going to require hard work, and it isn't going to be easy to get done."Michigan Representative Kristen McDonald Rivet agreed, saying she did not care "if we have to put Donald Trump's name" on legislation to gain the president's support for efforts to help her district.Tahra Hoops, the 28-year-old senior director of economic analysis at the Chamber of Progress, a "left-of-centre" tech think tank, suggested that the party's divisions be embraced, not paved over."I think Democrats can look different wherever they are," she said.While "very progressive" candidates can win in her home town of New York City, she said it made sense that Talarico held more centrist views because running in Texas "is not going to be the same"."America is a very diverse country; our politicians and their views should also be diverse," she added.Carlos Repetto-Ayala, a campaign consultant, made a similar point. The 25-year-old Texan travelled with two friends to the What's Next? event, wearing a cowboy hat and a red-white-and-blue pin on his lapel in the shape of the Lone Star State."It is a big tent party, but I think, as long as everyone that's in the party is laser-focused on addressing the issues that people would like for them to fix, I think Democrats will be successful," he said.

schema.headline: 'Frustrated' - Democrats remain a divided party despite winning big in midterms

title: Anthropic: The seven founders about to become multi-billionaires
description: Image source, David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei are chief executive and president
body: Image source, David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei are chief executive and president of AnthropicByTom Espiner and Lucy HookerBusiness reportersIn the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at $83 each, it said on Wednesday. At that price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $19.3bn (£14.7bn) each.So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?Dario Amodei - $19.7bnImage source, Finn Gomez/Getty ImagesIn 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT. He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".Listen: Dario Amodei BBC Sounds profileDaniela Amodei - $19.8bnImage source, Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesDario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.Tom Brown - $20bnImage source, Cornell Watson/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesTom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.Jack Clark - $19.8bnImage source, Peerapon Boonyakiat/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty ImagesJack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.Jared Kaplan - $19.8bnImage source, Chris J. Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesJared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.Chris Olah - $19.9bn Image source, Alberto PIZZOLI / AFP via Getty ImagesChris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum. Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain. The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.Sam McCandlish - $19.9bnImage source, AnthropicSam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.Figure caption, Power players: How do you value Anthropic?

title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in first-of-its kind IPO
description: Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the public stock market, taking its valu
body: Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the public stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion.The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 per share, showing there is plenty of excitement around AI.Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.5, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day, with shares hitting $97.Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet (down 3%) and Amazon (down 3.9%).The build-out happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble."Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate more quickly tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet.It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market."There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth $1.5 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available."We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.On Thursday, the same day Anthropic went public, a bipartisan group of lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product"."AI carries real risks," she added.Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

schema.headline: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in first-of-its kind IPO

title: Fiona the hippo dies after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo
description: "We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn
body: "We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore."Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, had said that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening."We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.While she seemed fine at first, her appetite started to decrease a few days later, and the zoo staff tried to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.An ultrasound before her death showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine. A zookeeper said surgery was not an option for full-grown hippos and "our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own".The zoo also tried a different approach to attempt to get the hat to pass by encouraging Fiona to stand on a vibration plate platform borrowed from a local horse farm."Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her.  They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Jenike said. Fiona was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo in 2017 and at first struggled to survive. At birth, she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.

schema.headline: Fiona the hippo dies after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo

title: Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
description: US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following
body: US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".Trump praised the trilateral meeting calling it "a great and highly consequential trip", in a social media post while flying back to Washington on Air Force One.In the same post, the president announced  he would host a news conference to talk about the trip on Friday at the White House. While in China, Trump met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend". He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.Meanwhile, Trump closed by saying the presidents of three of the world's largest countries have a "special responsibility" to maintain productive dialogue."Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said, adding: "We feel the opposite."Trump referenced the three countries' nuclear capabilities and said they are "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth".It is "vital" that they co-operate to "combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world", he said, adding: "That's what we're doing in Iran.""We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon".Trump then turned to Ukraine and said he and Putin have had a "long discussion" on the conflict there already.He added that Putin "and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war".Putin addressed the media following the trilateral meeting and described it as an "important chapter in the history of diplomacy".He said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict in Ukraine - but he said Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to better understand Europe's position.As the talks were under way in China, and even as Putin was holding his press conference claiming to be ready for peace, Ukraine's capital Kyiv was under attack from Russian drones.Putin has repeatedly rejected all ceasefire offers from Ukraine, insisting on his maximalist demands which Kyiv and its European allies say are tantamount to de facto capitulation of Ukraine. In Shenzhen, the Kremlin leader also vowed a "far more painful" retaliation in response to Ukrainian attacks on the bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea. A missile and drone attack on Tuesday destroyed its central road section.There was no mention from Putin of almost five years of Russian attacks on power plants, bridges and residential buildings in Ukraine.The Russian president also directly addressed comparisons between his meeting with Trump and Xi and the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the US met towards the end of World War Two."Nobody divided up the world at Yalta. It simply codified the realities that had emerged after WW2."And when it comes to today's conflicts, the realities on the ground will have to be accepted."The Kremlin released a video showing Putin leaving the summit venue and saying goodbye to Xi."Thank you for organising this," Putin said. "I don't think anyone even expected everything to go so well."Meanwhile, China's president described his meeting with Putin and Trump as "positive, constructive, and highly productive", according to the country's state broadcaster CCTV.It added that Xi recalled "the history of fighting side-by-side during WW2", as the three leaders emphasised the importance of "cherishing the hard-won peace".Thursday's trilateral meeting was reportedly the idea of Putin.Some Russian newspapers called it a "diplomatic victory" as after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine many Western leaders were trying to isolate him.The summit also marked the first time since Russia's war in Ukraine began that Putin took part in an international gathering attended by leaders from countries including Canada, Japan and Australia.US lawmakers responded with frustration to Trump's warmth towards America's geopolitical adversaries."I was encouraged by some of the commitments that came out of the President's meetings in Asia, particularly the recognition that nuclear war must never be fought," Republican Senator John Curtis said in an emailed statement to the BBC.But Curtis also said he was concerned about Trump's approach to the foreign leaders, adding that "Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends"."We should not treat them as though they share our values or interests," Curtis, who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, added. "Doing so risks undermining our national security, weakening trust with our allies, and sending the wrong message about where America stands."Jeanne Shaheen, a ranking Democratic member on the same committee, chose harsher words in her comment. "President Trump's 'friend' is a murderous war criminal," she wrote on X.With additional reporting from Brandon Drenon

schema.headline: Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
